title: Indian Workers Begin Signing Payout Deals in €31 Million Milan Consulate Settlement
excerpt: Nearly 300 workers, most recruited in India, will receive an average of €50,000 each in back pay and damages after prosecutors found they were paid less than $2 an hour on the U.S. consulate construction site.
body:
• Indian workers who built the new U.S. consulate in Milan have begun signing payout deals under a nearly €31 million ($35 million) settlement with the American contractor.
  • Nearly 300 workers will receive an average of about €50,000 ($57,000) each, with some payouts reaching €90,000 ($102,000) in back pay and damages.
  • What this means for you: if you or a relative worked on the Milan site through Caddell Construction or its recruiters and cooperated with investigators, check with the CGIL construction union or the court-appointed administrator about your eligibility; 265 workers have already received Italian residence permits tied to the case.
  • The criminal investigation against the contractor and two of its managers continues, and the company remains under court administration.

Indian workers who helped build the new U.S. consulate in Milan have begun signing payout agreements under a nearly €31 million ($35 million) settlement with the American construction firm that employed them — the next step after one of Europe's largest labour-exploitation settlements was announced late last month.

The settlement was signed by Milan prosecutors, Alabama-based Caddell Construction and the court-appointed administrator that took over the construction site after investigators moved in. About €19.7 million is earmarked for direct payments to workers in unpaid wages and damages for emotional distress; the remainder covers obligations to Italy's social security authorities and the labour inspectorate.

Paid less than $2 an hour

Prosecutors allege the workers — most of them recruited in India — were paid less than $2 an hour and hit with improper deductions for food and housing, far below what construction workers in Milan are entitled to under local labour agreements. The Carabinieri's labour-protection command carried out the inspections that led to the case.

Nearly 300 workers identified so far will receive on average €50,000 (about $57,000), with some receiving up to €90,000 ($102,000), Luca Stanzione, secretary general of the Milan branch of the CGIL trade union confederation, told The Associated Press. Unions involved in the case have described it as the largest settlement of its kind in Europe.

"The operation coordinated by the Milan Public Prosecutor's Office is one of the most significant in recent years against illegal labor brokering and labor exploitation."

— Marina Calderone, Italian Labour Minister

Context and background

The case centres on a 10-acre U.S. State Department construction site where Caddell Construction of Montgomery, Alabama, was the appointed contractor. The Associated Press also spoke to workers who said they had been recruited through a Caddell project at an American embassy facility in Africa, suggesting the labour-brokering chain spanned continents.

The case is striking because the alleged abuse happened on a U.S. government project, built by an American multinational, in Italy's financial capital. Calderone said the outcome proved the state would not abandon vulnerable workers.

Impact and analysis

Beyond the money, the settlement has produced concrete legal standing for the victims. Some 265 workers have now obtained Italian residence permits "for special reasons," according to the Ministry of Labour and Social Policies, with procedures underway for the rest. Undocumented workers who cooperate with prosecutors in Italy can obtain legal residence, making it far harder for them to be deported or re-exploited while the criminal case runs.

The criminal investigation against Caddell and two of its managers remains open, and the company stays under court administration — the payout does not close the book on corporate liability. The company did not respond to requests for comment when the settlement was announced.

The diaspora angle

The Milan settlement is a landmark for Indians recruited abroad by third-country employers. Workers who fly out on promises of fair wages often discover the deductions only after arrival, and fear of deportation keeps them silent. Here, workers who cooperated with authorities secured both back pay and legal residence — an outcome migrant-rights groups are already citing as a template. For Indian families considering overseas project work, the lesson is direct: insist on written contracts specifying net pay in the destination country's currency, keep copies of every document, and know that Italy's unions and labour inspectorate can be approached even by undocumented workers.

What's next

With payout deals now being signed, the money should begin flowing to workers in the coming weeks. The criminal case against the company and its managers will be the one to watch: a conviction would set a harder precedent for multinational contractors on European public projects.
